docs.title: Demo 2: VMware to OpenShift Virtualization (warm migration, storage copy offload)
docs.text:
Version 3.1.0 · draft · 2026-10-15 · class/demos/02-vmware-to-ove-warm.md

🚧 Coming soon. You can't run this demo in this lab yet.

This demo is written for a lab that has a supported SAN array with its CSI driver and snapshot support on OpenShift. This lab doesn't have one yet: its vSphere datastore is NFS and its OpenShift storage is ODF and NFS. Read it to learn how a warm migration works when the array copies the disks; it runs once the SAN is in.

What changed: the earlier Demo 2 used VMware's VDDK library. VDDK is no longer available to this lab, and this lab won't demo it again (why). Demo 2 now follows the path Red Hat points to: storage copy offload in MTV, with the VDDK-independent transfer Red Hat has in preview (status).

In class today: do Demo 1 (cold migration, no VDDK needed) and its bonus labs, then Demos 1c, 1d and 4.

docs.title: Why this lab does not demo VDDK
docs.text:
The Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK) is VMware's library for reading a VM's disks straight from ESXi. MTV used it to copy disks, and for a warm migration to copy only the blocks that changed while the VM ran. This lab built Demo 2 on it, and has stopped:

  1. We can't get it. Broadcom pulled the old VMware download links. VDDK now sits behind a Broadcom sign-in and entitlement, and the lab couldn't obtain the kit it was built for (vmware-vix-disklib-8.0.3).
  2. Nobody may hand it out. VDDK's licence doesn't let Red Hat, Paragon Micro or a class redistribute it. Each customer must download it under their own entitlement. A class built on it teaches a step most students can't repeat at home.
  3. Red Hat no longer leads with it. Red Hat's position (2026-10-14): a customer who already has a VDDK copy matching their VMware environment may still use it, once they confirm their right to keep and use the software; Red Hat then assesses its technical suitability. That's a bridge for existing customers, not a path to teach.
  4. There's a better path. MTV can have the storage array copy the disks (storage copy offload), and Red Hat is building a VDDK-independent transfer for both warm and cold migration. That is what this demo now teaches.

What still works without VDDK: cold migration. MTV reads the disks over vCenter/ESXi HTTPS instead: it's slower, and the VM is down for its whole disk copy. That's Demo 1, and it runs in this lab today.

The VDDK version of this guide (2.2.0) stays in the repository's history. The lab's VDDK automation (job vddk, Lab S §S.15) is retired.

docs.title: Where Red Hat is with this (2026-10-14)
docs.text:
Path Status Source Storage copy offload, cold generally available since MTV 2.11, with supported arrays and configurations MTV 2.11 planning guide Storage copy offload, warm Technology Preview in MTV 2.11; "fully supported" in MTV 2.12 (MTV-4562) MTV 2.12 release notes Warm migration without VDDK Developer Preview: Red Hat is testing a VDDK-independent transfer for warm and cold, "for controlled evaluation and not yet for production use" Red Hat, 2026-10-14 CSI volume import (the array clones VVol/RDM disks itself) Developer Preview in MTV 2.12.2 (MTV-5483) MTV 2.12 release notes An existing VDDK copy may remain a technical option; the customer confirms the right to use it Red Hat, 2026-10-14

[verify] before this demo ships: which of these the lab's MTV version gives, and whether a warm offload migration still needs VDDK for any step (for example the changed-block rounds). Confirm both with Red Hat for the chosen array.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
You move your Windows Server + PostgreSQL VM off VMware vSphere and onto OpenShift Virtualization while it keeps running. This time the SAN array does the copying: MTV asks the array, through its API and its CSI driver, to copy each disk into a new OpenShift volume on the same array, so the data never crosses the network. vSphere's Changed Block Tracking (CBT) and snapshots tell MTV what changed between rounds. The VM stops only for the cutover. Then you snapshot the migrated VM on the array, through OpenShift.

Phase Your VM What happens Pre-copy 1 running MTV snapshots each disk on vSphere; ESXi sends XCOPY and the array copies the whole disk into the new volume Pre-copy 2, 3, … running every 5 minutes, only the blocks changed since the last round (CBT) Cutover stopped one last snapshot and copy, the drivers converted, the VM started on OpenShift After running on OpenShift a VM snapshot, taken by the array through the CSI driver

docs.title: What this demo needs (this lab doesn't have it yet)
docs.text:
Piece What it must be In this lab today The SAN array one MTV supports for offload: Hitachi Vantara, NetApp ONTAP, Pure FlashArray, Dell PowerMax, PowerFlex or PowerStore, HPE 3PAR or Primera, Infinidat InfiniBox, IBM FlashSystem none (coresan01 is a Linux iSCSI/NFS appliance: no offload plugin) The source datastore VMFS on a LUN from that array, over iSCSI or FC, on every ESXi host coresan01_data00, NFS The CSI driver the array vendor's driver on site A, with a StorageClass on the same array (block volumes) ODF and nfs-csi Snapshots a VolumeSnapshotClass for that driver, so OpenShift VM snapshots are array snapshots ODF's only Array API credentials a Secret MTV uses to map new volumes to the ESXi hosts — vSphere privileges MTV's role plus Red Hat's StorageOffloader privileges (datastore browse and low-level file operations; host advanced settings, query patch, storage partition configuration; global settings) MTV's role only ESXi clone method SSH (Red Hat's recommendation; MTV makes the key) or the VIB on every host — MTV feature_copy_offload on (the default), and a version with warm offload (see above) MTV 2.11

The example below uses NetApp ONTAP with its Trident CSI driver. Any array in the list works the same way, with its own product name and Secret keys.

Before you start (once the SAN is in): do Lab 0. You are signed in to the site A console, and every command runs in the console's Web Terminal (>_). Your VM must be running on vSphere, with its disks on the SAN datastore.

⚠ The commands are an example. Change these values to yours before you run them:

In the example Is the example's Replace with yours student-01-0024-012 class ID and project (student-01 on booking 0024-012) your class ID win-pg-s01 your VM (s + your student number); on OpenShift it lands as win-pg-s01-warm your VM 10.101.23.101 your VM's address, the SQL server (it keeps it on OpenShift) your VM's address, from Lab 0.1 vcenter01 / VLAN 23 your booking's vCenter (N = 1) and VLAN (22 + N) from your instructor's N san_vmfs01 · ontap-san · ontap-snapclass the SAN datastore, its StorageClass and VolumeSnapshotClass from your instructor

docs.title: 2.0 Inject: the demo has started
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'demo-started', 'Demo 2: warm migration, storage copy offload');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"   # read back: your rows so far, oldest first

✅ One row, stage = demo-started.

docs.title: 2.1 Check the link to vCenter, the offload storage map, and your warm plan
docs.text:
The lab staged a warm plan for you, ready but not started: d2-win-pg-s01 (d2-<your VM>). It lands your VM on site A as win-pg-s01-warm. What makes it an offload plan is its storage map.

Console (site A): Migration for Virtualization → Providers → ovedr-vcenter01. ✅ Ready and Connected.

Console: Migration for Virtualization → Storage maps → ovedr-vcenter01-offload.

✅ One row: source san_vmfs01 → target ontap-san, Offload plugin vSphere XCOPY, Storage product ontap, and a Storage secret. Every row of a plan's storage map must use offload or none may: MTV won't mix the two.

Console: Migration plans → d2-win-pg-s01. ✅ Type Warm, your VM, the storage map ovedr-vcenter01-offload. The status is not Ready yet: expand your VM to see why.

Concern What it means Who fixes it VMMissingChangedBlockTracking your VM's disks don't have CBT on, so MTV can't find the changes you, in 2.2

The same from the Web Terminal [verify]:

oc -n openshift-mtv get storagemap ovedr-vcenter01-offload -o jsonpath='{range .spec.map[*]}{.source.name}{" -> "}{.destination.storageClass}{"  "}{.offloadPlugin.vsphereXcopyConfig.storageVendorProduct}{"\n"}{end}'   # san_vmfs01 -> ontap-san  ontap
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}{"\n"}{end}'

docs.title: 2.2 Turn on Changed Block Tracking, and clear old snapshots
docs.text:
CBT is one switch for the VM (ctkEnabled) plus one for each disk (scsi0:N.ctkEnabled). vCenter accepts them only while the VM is off.

Shut it down. vCenter: win-pg-s01 → Actions → Power → Shut Down Guest OS. Wait for Powered Off.

Delete old snapshots. win-pg-s01 → Snapshots → Manage Snapshots → delete any you find. A VM that already has snapshots leaves a delta chain that stops the array from doing the copy (ESXi falls back to a slower software copy). The snapshots MTV takes during the warm rounds don't matter.

Add the four parameters. win-pg-s01 → Edit Settings → Advanced Parameters. For each row, type the Attribute and Value, then click ADD:

Attribute Value ctkEnabled true scsi0:0.ctkEnabled true scsi0:1.ctkEnabled true scsi0:2.ctkEnabled true

Adding a row: Attribute ctkEnabled, Value true, then ADD.

All four rows set: the VM, plus scsi0:0, scsi0:1 and scsi0:2 for its three disks. Click OK.

Power it back on: Actions → Power → Power On.

✅ Within a minute or two the plan d2-win-pg-s01 shows Ready:

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status}{"\n"}{end}'   # Ready=True

Give Windows a minute to start PostgreSQL, then check that the shutdown lost nothing:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ chain_ok = t.

docs.title: 2.3 Start the warm migration, and keep writing
docs.text:
Console (site A): Migration plans → d2-win-pg-s01 → Start → confirm.

Your VM keeps running on vSphere. For each disk MTV creates a volume on ontap-san and a populator pod that asks ESXi to clone the disk into it; the array does the copy. The plan's page shows the transfer method as storage copy offload, not VDDK.

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -w                                   # EXECUTING True (Ctrl-C)
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get pvc                                               # three volumes on ontap-san [verify]
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o yaml | grep -i xcopy              # xcopyUsed: the array did the copy [verify]

Give it something to copy. Write 500 rows while the disks copy:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_load('student-01-0024-012', 'warm-precopy-load', 500);"

✅ rows_written = 500. Your VM is still serving its database in the middle of the migration.

Count the pre-copies:

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -o jsonpath='pre-copies done: {.status.migration.vms[0].warm.successes}  next: {.status.migration.vms[0].warm.nextPrecopyAt}{"\n"}'

✅ Wait for at least two. Compare how long the first took with a cold copy over the network in Demo 1.

Or: create and start your own warm offload plan from the CLI (instead of the staged one)

A new plan, so the staged one stays as the lab built it. Use one of them: a VM can be in only one running plan.

# your class ID: MTV creates your VM in this project on site A
CLASS_ID=student-01-0024-012
# your VM's name in vCenter
VM=win-pg-s01
# the provider that links site A to your booking's vCenter ("ovedr-vcenter0" + N)
SRC=ovedr-vcenter01
# a NEW plan name, so this never touches the staged d2-win-pg-s01
PLAN=$CLASS_ID-warm-cli

The plan is a normal warm plan; the offload storage map is what makes the array do the copy:

oc apply -f - <<EOT
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  warm: true
  targetNamespace: $CLASS_ID
  provider:
    source:      { name: $SRC, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    network: { name: $SRC-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: $SRC-offload,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms:
    - { name: $VM, targetName: $VM-warm-cli }
EOT
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # READY True (Ctrl-C)
oc apply -f - <<EOT
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Migration
metadata: { name: $PLAN-run1, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { plan: { name: $PLAN, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
EOT

In 2.4, after your start-warm-migration row, cut over now:

oc -n openshift-mtv patch migration $PLAN-run1 --type merge -p "{\"spec\":{\"cutover\":\"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)\"}}"
oc -n openshift-mtv get plan $PLAN -w                # SUCCEEDED True (Ctrl-C)

docs.title: 2.4 Inject, then cut over
docs.text:
Write the "start" row while your VM still runs on vSphere. It must survive the cutover:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'start-warm-migration', 'on vSphere, before cutover');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"   # read back: your rows so far, oldest first

Console (site A): Migration plans → d2-win-pg-s01 → Cutover → keep now → Set cutover.

MTV shuts your VM down on vSphere, takes one last snapshot, copies the last change, converts the drivers (virt-v2v installs virtio and the QEMU guest agent, and removes VMware Tools) and creates your VM on OpenShift.

oc -n openshift-mtv get plan d2-win-pg-s01 -w                        # SUCCEEDED True (Ctrl-C)

✅ Succeeded.

docs.title: 2.5 Review your VM on OpenShift, and snapshot it on the array
docs.text:
Console (site A): Virtualization → VirtualMachines, project student-01-0024-012 → win-pg-s01-warm.

Tab What you see Configuration → Network one NIC on default/vmnet23, so it keeps its address Configuration → Storage three disks on ontap-san: the SAN volumes the array copied into

✅ Running, guest agent connected, address 10.101.23.101.

Snapshot it, on the array. Snapshots → Take snapshot → name after-warm → Save. OpenShift asks the CSI driver, and the array takes the snapshot of each disk in place.

oc -n student-01-0024-012 get vmsnapshot                              # after-warm  Succeeded [verify]
oc -n student-01-0024-012 get volumesnapshot -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CLASS:.spec.volumeSnapshotClassName,READY:.status.readyToUse   # ontap-snapclass  true

✅ Three volume snapshots, class ontap-snapclass, ready. Demo 1a shows what you can do with one.

docs.title: 2.6 Inject: the migration is complete, read back, and measure the outage
docs.text:
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_mark('student-01-0024-012', 'warm-migration-complete', 'on OpenShift site A, SAN');"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, payload FROM marks ORDER BY id;"
oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify('student-01-0024-012');"

✅ The read-back ends with demo-started, the 500 warm-precopy-load rows, start-warm-migration and warm-migration-complete. chain_ok = t: nothing written during the copy was lost, changed or reordered.

The real outage, from your VM's heartbeat (a row every 5 seconds):

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -c "SELECT ts AS back_at, date_trunc('second', gap) AS outage FROM (SELECT ts, ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap FROM heartbeat) g WHERE gap > interval '10 seconds' AND ts > (SELECT max(ts) FROM marks WHERE student = 'student-01-0024-012' AND stage = 'start-warm-migration') ORDER BY ts;"

✅ One row: the cutover outage, minutes rather than the whole copy.

The guest tools were swapped:

oc exec -n student-01-0024-012 deploy/sql-client -- sql -h 10.101.23.101 -x -c "SELECT ts, platform, vmtools, qemu_ga, virtio FROM guest_tools ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1;"

✅ qemu_ga Running, virtio drivers listed, vmtools not running.

That is the end of Demo 2. Your VM moved while it kept writing, the array did the copying, and the array holds its first snapshot on OpenShift.

docs.title: Addendum: how the lab will stage this demo, as code
docs.text:
Not built yet: it waits on the SAN. The provider, the network map and the CI pipeline stay as Demo 1's (Demo 1 addendum). Offload adds:

Piece What it declares the SAN fabric a VMFS datastore on an array LUN for every ESXi host; the vendor's CSI driver, StorageClass and VolumeSnapshotClass on site A mtv-install the 5-minute pre-copy interval, and feature_copy_offload on mtv-fabric the StorageOffloader privileges on MTV's vSphere role; esxiCloneMethod: ssh on the provider; the array Secret; the offload storage map stage the warm plan d2-<vm> on the offload map, landing as <vm>-warm 
# the array's API credentials, which MTV uses to map new volumes to ESXi (keys vary by vendor)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: { name: ovedr-san-offload, namespace: openshift-mtv }
stringData:
  GOVMOMI_HOSTNAME: vcenter01.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com
  GOVMOMI_USERNAME: ovedr-mtv@vsphere.local
  GOVMOMI_PASSWORD: <from the lab's secret store>
  STORAGE_HOSTNAME: <the array's management address>
  STORAGE_USERNAME: <array user>
  STORAGE_PASSWORD: <from the lab's secret store>
  ONTAP_SVM: <the SVM that serves the LUNs>          # NetApp only
---
# the provider: the clone method is the only change from Demo 1's
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Provider
metadata: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  type: vsphere
  url: https://vcenter01.demo.lab-paragonmicro.com/sdk
  secret: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  settings:
    esxiCloneMethod: ssh                              # or vib; no vddkInitImage
---
# the offload storage map: the SAN datastore -> the SAN's StorageClass, copied by the array
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageMap
metadata: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-offload, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  provider:
    source:      { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv }
  map:
    - source: { name: san_vmfs01 }
      destination: { storageClass: ontap-san }
      offloadPlugin:
        vsphereXcopyConfig: { secretRef: ovedr-san-offload, storageVendorProduct: ontap }
---
# the staged warm plan, on the offload map
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Plan
metadata: { name: d2-win-pg-s01, namespace: openshift-mtv, labels: { ovedr/stage: plan, ovedr/type: warm } }
spec:
  warm: true
  targetNamespace: student-01-0024-012
  provider: { source: { name: ovedr-vcenter01, namespace: openshift-mtv }, destination: { name: host, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
  map:
    network: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-net-bridge, namespace: openshift-mtv }
    storage: { name: ovedr-vcenter01-offload,    namespace: openshift-mtv }
  vms: [ { name: win-pg-s01, targetName: win-pg-s01-warm } ]

The Secret, StorageMap and Provider fields follow Red Hat's guide and MTV's upstream populator; [verify] each one on the lab's MTV version and array.

What stays hands-on, on purpose: CBT and clearing old snapshots (2.2), starting the plan and the cutover (2.3, 2.4), and the snapshot on the array (2.5).

docs.title: Demo 4: ODF Regional-DR
docs.text: Version 0.6.1 · draft · 2026-10-16 · class/demos/04-odf-regional-dr.md

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: You will protect running virtual machines with OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) Regional-DR, which replicates their disks asynchronously from site A to site B every 15 minutes. You will prove that a replication cycle really completed, by injecting rows into PostgreSQL and watching them reach the other site. You will move the VMs to site B and home again without losing a single row, and you will see that only the changes travel, not whole disks. In the bonus round you break the replication link, force a failover and measure exactly what an unplanned disaster costs (the RPO).

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
How the two clusters are joined (ACM hub, Submariner, then ODF's MirrorPeer/DRPolicy), what this lab has today and what CI automates: Lab S §S.14. Read it first: this demo depends on all three layers.

The booking's CI customization (the dr-fabric and dr-policy jobs, which run when DR is on) built all of this before class. See the lab diagram, and Lab S — how this lab was built for the CLI and console steps behind the shared pieces.

Pre-built Where How to check How it was built · Red Hat docs ODF on BOTH sites (storage: odf on site A and site B, an operator toggle on the booking) site A, site B oc --context site-X -n openshift-storage get storagecluster → Ready on both S.4 · ODF 4.19 ACM and cert-manager on both clusters (demo-openshift's base build, the same operators on both). DR runs from site B's hub, with site A imported as a managed cluster site B oc --context site-b get managedclusters S.10 · ACM 2.16 ODF Multicluster Orchestrator and the DR hub operator (Ramen) on the hub, and the DR cluster operator on both sites site B / both §4.2 ODF DR guide Submariner (the network tunnel Ceph mirrors over; Globalnet and the provider-server export only if the sites' IPv4 ranges overlap), the MirrorPeer, both DRClusters both §4.2 ODF DR guide: Regional-DR The same VLAN bridges on both sites: every vmnet<VLAN> your VMs use exists on site A and site B, same name, same VLAN. A Relocate or Failover brings back the VM's own definition, which names its bridge (default/vmnet23): without that bridge on the other site the VM doesn't start, and with it the VM keeps its address both oc --context site-a -n default get net-attach-def and the same on site-b: the same vmnet* names demo-openshift's VLAN build on each site (BL-B29) The 15-minute DRPolicy (sync_interval=15m) site B §4.2 §4.2 Your namespace with your browser terminal sql-client and your VM's Service (<VM>-sql); ovedr-app with the instructor's, on both sites both oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get deploy,svc S.9 Your own VM ($VM, e.g. win-pg-s03) running on site A, on ODF storage (ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization), at its own address $VM_IP on the VLAN bridge (Demo 1's staged plan) site A where → site-a Running S.11 · S.12 Your Windows login (.\<WINUSER>) and the PostgreSQL toolkit (marks, ovedr_*) inside your VM your VM verify S.11

docs.title: Who is in charge: the hub supervises, the sites are not peers
docs.text:
Two clusters, but they don't have equal roles. One ACM hub supervises both. Only the hub can protect a VM, run a Relocate or a Failover, or show the whole picture. In this lab the hub is on site B (ocp-lz2 in the examples).

Cluster Its role What its console's All Clusters → Clusters shows Site B (ocp-lz2) the hub (ACM, ODF Multicluster Orchestrator, Ramen's DR hub operator), and a managed cluster (local-cluster), and the DR target both clusters, Ready Site A (ocp-lz1) a managed cluster only: runs the VMs, the DR cluster operator, and mirrors its disks to B nothing, by design: ACM lets a cluster belong to only one hub, and site A's belongs to site B's

What the hub knows while a site is down. A hub can't see a cluster that is down. It shows that cluster as Unknown and keeps what it last heard: each protected namespace's DR state and its last completed sync. What failover needs is already on the surviving site: the disks' snapshots, mirrored there every interval, and the VM and volume definitions, which the DR operators keep in an object store on each site [verify: Ramen's S3 metadata store on ODF 4.19].

What fails Can you fail over? What to do Site A (the VMs' home) ✅ yes: the hub on B is up Failover to B from the hub (§4.8). When A is back, the hub sees it again, reverses replication, and you relocate home (§4.6). This is why the hub sits on B. Site B (the hub's site) ❌ no: nothing can drive a failover The VMs on A keep running, but replication to B stops and no Relocate or Failover can run. Bring the hub back online first: once it's up, it reconnects to A, replication resumes, and you can manage the other cluster again. The hub, for good ❌ not until a hub exists again Restore the hub's backup onto another cluster (ACM's hub backup and restore, with a passive hub kept ready), then carry on from it [verify].

⚠ A lab compromise. Red Hat's supported Regional-DR layout has three clusters: the hub on its own, away from both sites, usually with a passive standby hub. Then losing either site never costs you the hub. This lab has two clusters, so the hub shares site B. That's fine for the disaster this demo shows (site A lost), but the first step of any recovery is getting the hub back: it's the cluster you manage all the others from. ACM: hub backup and restore [verify link].

What you do yourself: inspect every DR layer, inject and verify data at every stage, read replication status at three levels, and run the moves when you are the driver.

⚠ Capacity, stated plainly. Each ODF cluster takes all 4 scratch SSDs, one on each demosvr host. Today the lab has 4, so it can run one ODF site. Every other demo runs with site A on ODF and site B on NFS. Demo 4 needs a booking with ODF on both sites, which becomes possible when the additional drives are installed. Until then, run this demo from the 📸 screenshots only.

One protection unit for the whole class. Each student's VM lives in that student's own namespace (their class ID), the instructor's in ovedr-app. The default is one DRPC protecting all of them: ovedr-app plus every student namespace [verify: a discovered-app DRPC with several protectedNamespaces]. Every Relocate or Failover moves every student's VM together, so 🧑‍🏫 the driver runs the DR actions, and each of you verifies your own VM. Per-VM protection (one DRPC per student VM, selecting that VM's disks by label) is possible but not built here [verify].

Before you start: do Lab 0, then sign your class terminal in on both sites and to your database (Toolkit T.1-T.2: oclogin for site A and site B, then dblogin). It already holds the variables ($ME, $N, $A, $B, $VM, $VM_IP, $WINUSER) and the commands (sql, mark, load, verify, alive, where).

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal. Every bash block in this guide runs in your own terminal pod, in the browser: in the site A console, project <your class ID> → Workloads → Pods → sql-client → Terminal (Toolkit T.1). Nothing is installed on your computer. It already knows your VM and its address (type ovedr); dblogin and oclogin (Toolkit T.1-T.2) stay signed in while the pod runs. Variables you export last until you close that Terminal tab: if you reopen it, re-run the guide's export lines. Paste with right-click → Paste (or Ctrl+Shift+V / ⌘V). powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console (vCenter Launch Web Console, or the VM's Console tab in OpenShift).

🎬 Video: Demo 4: ODF Regional-DR

🎬 Demo 4: ODF Regional-DR: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 4.0 Point the helpers at your VM
docs.text:
Use your VM's own address, $VM_IP, for every connection test. Your VM sits on the VLAN bridge (vmnet<VLAN>), which exists with the same name on both sites, so after a Relocate or Failover it comes up with the same address on the other site. (Only a VM on the pod network gets a new pod IP per site: then refresh it with Toolkit T.4 after every move.) Your VM's Service ($VM-sql) also follows the VM between sites.

export PGHOST=$VM_IP                                  # or: export PGHOST=$VM-sql
export DRPC=ovedr-app                                 # the class's one DRPC (ovedr-app + every student namespace)
# the DR state of the class's protected namespace, read from the hub (site B)
drpc() { oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" \
           -o jsonpath='{"phase="}{.status.phase}{"  progression="}{.status.progression}{"  lastSync="}{.status.lastGroupSyncTime}{"  dur="}{.status.lastGroupSyncDuration}{"  bytes="}{.status.lastGroupSyncBytes}{"\n"}'; }
# Ceph's own view of mirroring, on one site (needs rsh into the tools pod: instructor screen if your role cannot)
rbdmirror() { oc --context "$1" -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
                rbd mirror pool status ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool --verbose; }

where; alive
mark d4-start
verify

✍️ Row 4.0: your d4-start mark id and the fingerprint.

docs.title: 4.2 Set up asynchronous replication between the clusters
docs.text:
Regional-DR is built in layers. The lab stages the lower ones (dr-fabric); you inspect each one and see what it is for.

Layer Object (on the hub unless noted) What it does Cluster set ManagedClusterSet, both ManagedClusters ACM knows both sites Network Submariner Broker + add-on on each cluster a tunnel between the clusters' networks, which carries Ceph's mirror traffic Storage peering MirrorPeer (ODF Multicluster Orchestrator) turns on RBD mirroring between the two Ceph clusters and exchanges their keys and S3 stores DR clusters DRCluster ×2 (created by the MirrorPeer) Ramen's view of each site and its S3 store Policy DRPolicy which two clusters pair up, and how often to checkpoint 
oc --context site-b get managedclusters                                   # ocp-lzX, ocp-lzY (+ local-cluster): JOINED, AVAILABLE
oc --context site-b get managedclusteraddons -A | grep -E 'submariner|NAME'
oc --context site-b get mirrorpeer -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TYPE:.spec.type,PHASE:.status.phase
oc --context site-b get drcluster \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,S3:.spec.s3ProfileName,VALIDATED:'.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Validated")].status'

Submariner links the two sites' pod and service networks. If the sites have separate ranges (the plan), it runs without Globalnet. If only their IPv4 ranges overlap, it runs with Globalnet, and each site exports ODF's provider server so the two Ceph clusters can find each other (Lab S §S.14 layer 2):

oc --context site-b -n ovedr-broker get broker submariner-broker -o jsonpath='{.spec.globalnetEnabled}{"\n"}'   # false (true only for an IPv4 overlap)
for s in site-a site-b; do
  echo "== $s"
  oc --context $s -n openshift-storage get storageclusterpeer -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATE:.status.state   # Peered
  oc --context $s -n openshift-storage get cephblockpoolradosnamespaces ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool-builtin-implicit \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.mirroringStatus.summary}{"\n"}'                   # "daemon_health":"OK", "health":"OK"
done
Example code: how the lab built these layers (instructor)

The full commands, layer by layer, with the console path for each: Lab S §S.14. CI runs them as dr_fabric.sh (Submariner, MCG, the provider-server export when Globalnet is on, the Orchestrator, the MirrorPeer) and dr_policy.sh (the 15-minute DRPolicy) on every booking with ODF on both sites.

Debug: a layer is missing or unhealthy What you see Look at Fix no mirrorpeer or drcluster at all the booking's dr-fabric job the booking isn't ODF on both sites (storage: odf), or dr-fabric failed: its log names the step Submariner add-on not AVAILABLE oc --context site-b -n <cluster> get managedclusteraddon submariner -o yaml Lab S §S.14 layer 2 debug: gateway node label, UDP 4500 between the gateway nodes storageclusterpeer missing or not Peered oc --context site-X -n openshift-storage get serviceexport ocs-provider-server -o yaml the provider-server export and StorageCluster annotation (Lab S §S.14 layer 3, step 2) mirroring health WARNING wait: a new link takes up to 10 minutes still WARNING/ERROR after that: Lab S §S.14 layer 3 debug

docs.title: 🧑‍🏫 Driver: the 15-minute DRPolicy
docs.text:
The user-facing promise of this demo is "a checkpoint every 15 minutes". That is the schedulingInterval.

export POLICY=$A-$B-15m
cat <<YAML | oc --context site-b apply -f -
apiVersion: ramendr.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: DRPolicy
metadata: { name: $POLICY }
spec:
  drClusters: [ $A, $B ]
  schedulingInterval: 15m
  replicationClassSelector: {}
  volumeSnapshotClassSelector: {}
YAML

The interval must be one the MirrorPeer offers (spec.schedulingIntervals). The lab's MirrorPeer offers 2m, 5m and 15m, and CI has usually created this policy already (dr_policy.sh), so the apply just confirms it.

Debug: the DRPolicy stays validated=False 
oc --context site-b get drpolicy "$POLICY" -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.reason}: {.message}{"\n"}{end}'
oc --context site-b get mirrorpeer -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.schedulingIntervals}{"\n"}'      # must include 15m
oc --context site-b get drcluster -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,VALIDATED:'.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Validated")].status'

An interval the MirrorPeer doesn't offer, or a drClusters name that isn't a DRCluster (ocp-<A>, local-cluster), are the usual causes. One DRPolicy per interval; you can't edit an existing policy's interval (Red Hat ODF 4.19).

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
oc --context site-b get drpolicy "$POLICY" \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedulingInterval}{"  validated="}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Validated")].status}{"\n"}'
# the per-interval replication classes the MirrorPeer created on each site
for s in site-a site-b; do echo "== $s"; oc --context $s get volumereplicationclass; done

✅ 15m validated=True. ✅ Each site has a VolumeReplicationClass whose schedulingInterval is 15m.

📸 04-drpolicy: the DRPolicy validated at 15m.

docs.title: 4.3 Protect the VM
docs.text: mark d4-before-protect

docs.title: 🧑‍🏫 Driver: enrol the VM
docs.text:
The VMs were created by MTV, not by a GitOps application, so they are a discovered application. Protect ovedr-app (the instructor's VM and sql-client) and every student namespace (each student's VM, its disks and its Service), so a move carries everything the class uses.

Console, site B (hub): All Clusters → Data Services → Disaster recovery → Protected applications → Enroll discovered application [verify: BL-T07]: - cluster $A - namespaces ovedr-app and every student-NN-<booking> namespace - policy $POLICY - resources: all in namespace - kube-object capture interval 15m

That creates the Placement and the DRPlacementControl (DRPC) on the hub. As YAML, roughly [verify]:

apiVersion: ramendr.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: DRPlacementControl
metadata: { name: ovedr-app, namespace: openshift-dr-ops }
spec:
  preferredCluster: <A>
  drPolicyRef: { name: <A>-<B>-15m }
  placementRef: { kind: Placement, name: ovedr-app-placement, namespace: openshift-dr-ops }
  protectedNamespaces: [ ovedr-app, student-01-<booking>, student-02-<booking> ]   # one entry per student namespace [verify]
  pvcSelector: {}
  kubeObjectProtection: { captureInterval: 15m, kubeObjectSelector: {} }

docs.title: Check: the first sync is a FULL copy
docs.text:
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o wide -w          # Ctrl-C at Deployed / Protected
drpc
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get volumereplicationgroup                 # one VRG, state Primary
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get volumereplicationgroup "$DRPC" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.reason}{"\n"}{end}'

✅ The VRG reports DataReady=True, DataProtected=True and ClusterDataProtected=True [verify: condition names on ODF 4.19]. ✍️ Row 4.3: the first lastGroupSyncBytes and lastGroupSyncDuration. This is the only full copy in the demo. Compare it with the VM's disk usage (oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc).

📸 04-protected: the Protected applications page showing ovedr-app Healthy.

docs.title: 4.4 Prove replication is running, and that a cycle completed
What "running" looks like, at three levels
docs.text:
drpc                                                           # 1 · Ramen: the last group sync
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get volumereplication          # 2 · CSI: one VolumeReplication per disk
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get volumereplication \
  -o custom-columns=PVC:.spec.dataSource.name,STATE:.status.state,LASTSYNC:.status.lastSyncTime
rbdmirror site-a                                               # 3 · Ceph: images up+stopped (primary), health OK
rbdmirror site-b                                               #     images up+replaying (secondary)

To see one image's mirror snapshots, which are the checkpoints themselves:

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc | grep "$VM"              # your VM's three disks: pick one
PVC='<one of your VM pvcs>'
IMG=$(oc --context site-a get pv "$(oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get pvc "$PVC" -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}')" \
        -o jsonpath='{.spec.csi.volumeAttributes.imageName}')
oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
  rbd mirror image status "ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool/$IMG"
oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
  rbd snap ls --all "ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool/$IMG" | grep -i mirror

✅ Primary: state: up+stopped, with description showing the last mirror snapshot. Secondary: up+replaying.

docs.title: Inject, then wait for ONE complete sync that contains your row
docs.text:
load d4-busy 200                                 # a burst: the database is busy
mark d4-wait-for-sync                            # the row that must reach site B
T=$(sql -Atc "SELECT max(ts) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME'")
echo "my row's time: $T"
# poll the hub until a group sync STARTED after your row's time (each sync is a crash-consistent snapshot)
until [ "$(date -d "$(oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o jsonpath='{.status.lastGroupSyncTime}')" +%s 2>/dev/null || echo 0)" \
        -gt "$(date -d "$T" +%s)" ]; do
  printf '%s  waiting… ' "$(date +%T)"; drpc; sleep 60
done
echo "✅ a sync completed after your row"; drpc

The loop uses GNU date -d, which your browser terminal (Linux) has.

💡 With a 15-minute interval this can take up to 15 minutes. That wait is the RPO you are buying. The instructor may use a 5-minute policy in a short session.

✅ lastGroupSyncTime is later than your row, so your d4-wait-for-sync row is now on site B's disks. ✍️ Row 4.4: a typical checkpoint's bytes and dur. Compare them with row 4.3: it should be a small fraction.

📸 04-sync-complete: the drpc line after the loop ends.

docs.title: 4.5 Snapshot, then a planned failover to site B
A snapshot as a local safety net
docs.text:
cat <<YAML | oc --context site-a apply -f -
apiVersion: snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata: { name: $VM-d4-pre-move, namespace: $VMNS }
spec:
  source: { apiGroup: kubevirt.io, kind: VirtualMachine, name: $VM }
YAML
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vmsnapshot "$VM-d4-pre-move" -w        # Ctrl-C at readyToUse=true

[verify] snapshot.kubevirt.io/v1beta1 is the served version on OpenShift Virtualization 4.19 (v1alpha1 on older releases).

💡 A snapshot is not DR. It lives on the same Ceph cluster as the VM. It protects against a bad change (Demo 1's bonus round), not against losing the site. Replication is what protects the site.

docs.title: Relocate vs Failover
docs.text:
Relocate (planned) Failover (unplanned) When both sites healthy: maintenance, evacuation, a test the primary is gone or unreachable Order stop the VM on A → final sync → demote A → promote B → start on B promote B from the last completed sync → start on B Data loss none up to one interval (the RPO)

A "clean migration" between sites is a Relocate. The bonus round does a real Failover.

docs.title: 🧑‍🏫 Driver: Relocate to site B
docs.text:
mark d4-before-relocate
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops patch drpc "$DRPC" --type merge \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"action\":\"Relocate\",\"preferredCluster\":\"$B\"}}"

(Console: Protected applications → ovedr-app → ⋮ → Relocate.)

docs.title: Check: on site B, nothing lost
docs.text:
Your VM came up on site B with the same address ($PGHOST), so the helpers work unchanged:

oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o wide -w           # Relocating → Relocated
where                                                                        # site-b Running
oc --context site-b -n "$VMNS" get vm,vmi,pvc,svc,deploy                   # everything came with it
alive
verify
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, stage FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5;"

✅ d4-before-relocate is present on site B, so a planned move loses nothing. ✅ chain_ok = t. The fingerprint equals the one you would get on A at the moment it stopped. ✍️ Row 4.5: Relocate duration (DRPC lastGroupSyncDuration, plus the heartbeat gap from alive) and rows lost (0).

Your file, in the console on site B:

Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" -Tail 3        # d4-start is there
Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d4 on site B"

📸 04-on-site-b: where showing site-b, and the file's tail.

docs.title: 4.6 Reverse replication B → A, then come home cleanly
docs.text:
The VM now runs on B, and B is the primary. Before you move it again, check that protection has reversed: B replicates back to A, and A's images are the secondaries.

mark d4-on-b
drpc
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.reason}{"\n"}{end}'
rbdmirror site-b            # B: up+stopped (primary)
rbdmirror site-a            # A: up+replaying (secondary): the reverse direction is live

✅ PeerReady=True and Protected=True. ✅ A's images are up+replaying. Wait for one sync after d4-on-b, using the same loop as §4.4, with site-b in place of site-a in the sql call.

docs.title: 🧑‍🏫 Driver: Relocate home to site A
docs.text:
mark d4-before-home
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops patch drpc "$DRPC" --type merge \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"action\":\"Relocate\",\"preferredCluster\":\"$A\"}}"
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o wide -w

docs.title: Check: the VM is home, and the data made the full round trip
docs.text:
Same address again, now on site A:

where                                            # site-a Running
alive
verify
sql -c "SELECT stage, count(*), min(id), max(id) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' GROUP BY stage ORDER BY min(id);"
drpc                                             # Relocated; protection A → B again

✅ Every stage is present: d4-start, d4-busy (200 rows), d4-wait-for-sync, d4-before-protect, d4-before-relocate, d4-on-b and d4-before-home. ✅ chain_ok = t. ✍️ Row 4.6: the bytes of the return sync. It is a delta (what changed on B), not the whole disk.

Console on site A:

Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" -Tail 4        # both "site A" and "site B" lines

📸 04-home: verify with chain_ok = t, and the file's tail.

docs.title: 4.7 End-of-demo validation
docs.text:
alive
verify
sql -c "SELECT * FROM ovedr_verify();"                        # the whole class: every student's chain_ok
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, date_trunc('second', gap) AS outage FROM (
                 SELECT id, ts, ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS gap FROM heartbeat) g
               WHERE gap > interval '10 seconds' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5;"   # each move's outage (RTO)
Row Stage Bytes Duration Rows lost Your last mark id chain_ok Fingerprint 4.0 start — — — 4.3 first sync (full) — 4.4 typical 15-min checkpoint — 4.5 Relocate A → B 0 4.6 Relocate B → A (home) 0

The claim holds if rows 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6 are each a small fraction of row 4.3, and every planned move lost zero rows.

🧑‍🏫 Optional cleanup: oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" delete vmsnapshot "$VM-d4-pre-move".

docs.title: 4.8 BONUS: a hostile failover, with a broken replication link
docs.text: Now the link fails, the business can't wait, and the class forces the VM onto site B from whatever the last completed sync holds. Then it repairs the link and forces the resync back.

docs.title: How to break the link: options
docs.text:
Option What happens Realism Risk Recovery A. Cut the Submariner tunnel (recommended) 🧑‍🏫 Ceph mirror traffic stops. Both clusters stay up, and ACM still talks to both "the WAN link died" low: one label on one node put the label back B. Power off all site-A nodes 🧑‍🏫 (virsh destroy, instructor guide §4.1) site A vanishes entirely "the site burned down" medium: Ceph on A restarts from a crash virsh start; wait for Ceph HEALTH_OK C. Scale down rbd-mirror on site B the secondary stops pulling narrow: a storage fault rook/ocs operators scale it back up unless they are paused too scale the operators back up D. Fence site A (DRCluster spec.clusterFence: Fenced) Metro-DR only. Regional-DR does not fence [verify] — — not used

Recommended: option A. It matches "break the ODF sync link" exactly: replication fails while both sites still run, so the class sees a link failure rather than a site loss. It is reversed with one command. Option B is the scripted disaster in the classic M6 module.

docs.title: Step 1: inject, and note the last sync that got through
docs.text:
mark d4h-before-break
until [ "$(date -d "$(oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o jsonpath='{.status.lastGroupSyncTime}')" +%s)" \
        -gt "$(date -d "$(sql -Atc "SELECT max(ts) FROM marks WHERE student='$ME'")" +%s)" ]; do drpc; sleep 60; done
drpc                       # ✍️ lastSync = the last checkpoint that will reach B
sql -Atc "SELECT max(id) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME'"          # ✍️ your last SAFE id

docs.title: Step 2: 🧑‍🏫 break the link (option A) [verify]
docs.text:
# the gateway node(s) on site B carry the label submariner.io/gateway=true; removing it stops the tunnel
GW=$(oc --context site-b get nodes -l submariner.io/gateway=true -o name)
echo "$GW" > /tmp/ovedr-gw-site-b.txt
oc --context site-b label $GW submariner.io/gateway-
oc --context site-b -n submariner-operator get gateways -o wide      # no active gateway / connection error

docs.title: Step 3: keep writing on A. These rows will NOT reach B.
docs.text:
for n in 1 2 3; do mark "d4h-after-break-$n"; sleep 20; done
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, stage FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 4;"

✍️ Write down these ids and the first 12 characters of each sha. They are the rows you are about to lose.

# in your VM's console on site A
Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d4h written AFTER the link broke"

After one interval, the hub notices that syncs have stopped:

drpc                                                    # lastSync stops advancing
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.reason}{"\n"}{end}'

docs.title: Step 4: 🧑‍🏫 force Failover to site B
docs.text:
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops patch drpc "$DRPC" --type merge \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"action\":\"Failover\",\"failoverCluster\":\"$B\"}}"
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o wide -w        # FailingOver → FailedOver

ACM still reaches site A, so Ramen stops the VM there (it becomes the secondary) and starts it on B from the last completed sync.

docs.title: Step 5: measure what was lost (the RPO)
docs.text:
Same address, on site B:

where                                                   # site-b Running
verify
sql -c "SELECT id, ts, stage, left(sha,12) AS sha FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 4;"

What you should see, and why: - The last row present is your last SAFE id from step 1. Every d4h-after-break-* row is missing. - chain_ok is still t. A chain detects rows lost, changed or reordered in the middle. Losing the tail leaves a shorter chain that is still valid. That is why you wrote down your ids: your notes are the evidence of what the failover cost. - Write a new mark on B. Its id may reuse one of the lost ids, because B's sequence continues from the replicated state. Its sha differs from your note, so it is a different row with the same number.

mark d4h-on-b-after-failover
sql -c "SELECT id, stage, left(sha,12) FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2;"

# console on site B: the "AFTER the link broke" line is gone, because the disk is from the last sync
Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" -Tail 3

✍️ Row 4.8a: rows lost (count of d4h-after-break-*), RPO (failover time minus the last lastSync), and the outage (heartbeat gap on B).

📸 04-hostile-lost-rows: your noted ids beside B's marks tail.

docs.title: Step 6: 🧑‍🏫 restore the link and force the resync
docs.text:
oc --context site-b label $(cat /tmp/ovedr-gw-site-b.txt) submariner.io/gateway=true
oc --context site-b -n submariner-operator get gateways -o wide       # connected again
drpc                                                                  # progression moves on

If progression stops at WaitOnUserToCleanUp, the stale VM on site A must go before A can become the secondary. That is the instructor's cleanup, in instructor guide §4.3 [verify: BL-T09].

Then watch A's images become secondaries and catch up from the last common snapshot:

rbdmirror site-a          # A: syncing → up+replaying
rbdmirror site-b          # B: up+stopped (primary)

[verify: BL-T09] If an image stays in split-brain or error, Ceph needs an explicit resync of that image on the old primary (A). This copies the whole image, so use it only when Ramen does not recover by itself:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage rsh deploy/rook-ceph-tools \
  rbd mirror image resync "ocs-storagecluster-cephblockpool/<image>"

✍️ Row 4.8b: resync bytes and duration. A delta (from the last common checkpoint) proves the DESIGN's claim. A full copy means the hostile path costs one full copy, and the guide says so honestly (DESIGN §6.4).

docs.title: Step 7: 🧑‍🏫 Relocate home, and verify the history
docs.text:
mark d4h-before-home
# wait for one sync after that mark (§4.4 loop, site-b), then:
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops patch drpc "$DRPC" --type merge \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"action\":\"Relocate\",\"preferredCluster\":\"$A\"}}"
oc --context site-b -n openshift-dr-ops get drpc "$DRPC" -o wide -w
where
verify
sql -c "SELECT id, stage, left(sha,12) AS sha FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' AND stage LIKE 'd4h%' ORDER BY id;"

✅ Present: d4h-before-break, d4h-on-b-after-failover and d4h-before-home. ✅ Missing: every d4h-after-break-*. These were written only on A after the link broke, then discarded when A was resynced from B. That is exactly the data the hostile failover cost. ✅ chain_ok = t on A. The chain continues from the last safe row, through B, and home.

Row Stage Bytes Duration Rows lost Notes 4.8a forced Failover A ✗ → B — RPO = 4.8b resync after the link returns — delta or full? 4.8c Relocate home 0

📸 04-hostile-home: the final d4h% query on site A.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Regional-DR asynchronous replication between two clusters. RPO is greater than 0, at most one schedulingInterval MirrorPeer ODF Multicluster Orchestrator's pairing of two Ceph clusters, which turns on RBD mirroring DRPolicy the two clusters, and the checkpoint interval (here 15m) DRPC DRPlacementControl: the DR state of one protected workload, and where you ask for Relocate or Failover VRG VolumeReplicationGroup: the per-cluster agent that makes the workload's disks primary or secondary Relocate planned move: final sync, zero loss Failover forced move from the last completed sync: loss up to one interval RPO / RTO how much data you can lose / how long you are down

docs.title: Demo 5 (bonus): Back up and restore your VM with OADP
docs.text:
Version 0.2.1 · framework · 2026-10-12 · class/demos/05-oadp-vm-backup.md

🚧 Bonus, framework. OADP is now built by the lab when a class books it (option backup: oadp, the default for this class). The commands below are unproven [verify] until a booking has run them. Ask your instructor whether your lab has OADP before you start.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: Disaster recovery (Demo 4) keeps a running copy on another site. A backup is different: a point-in-time copy you can restore after a mistake, a bad change or a ransomware event, even when every replica has the damage too. You will back up your whole namespace with OADP (the OpenShift API for Data Protection, Red Hat's Velero-based operator): the VirtualMachine, its disks and its Service. Then you delete it all, restore it, and prove with your own rows that the restored VM holds exactly the data it had at backup time.

docs.title: How the lab is set up for this demo
docs.text:
Where What is pre-built (planned) How it is built Both sites (demo-openshift, backup: oadp) the OADP operator (1.5) in openshift-adp, a DataProtectionApplication with the openshift, aws, kubevirt and csi plugins, the node agent and the Data Mover (disk snapshots copied off the cluster), and non-admin backups: you back up and restore your own namespace yourself OADP [verify link] Both sites a backup location on the lab's object store (MinIO, outside the clusters), one bucket per cluster and a folder per booking: backups outlive the cluster Backup locations [verify link] You your VM running on site A (after Demo 1), in your namespace —

You do yourself: inject data, request a backup of your namespace, delete your VM, restore it, and verify.

🖥️ Where you type the commands: your browser terminal (Toolkit T.1), signed in on site A, with dblogin done. powershell blocks run inside your Windows VM, from its console.

🎬 Video: Demo 5: OADP backup and restore

🎬 Demo 5: OADP backup and restore: a walk-through of the whole demo in the console. Watch it, then do the same with the steps below.

docs.title: 5.1 What a VM backup contains
docs.text:
A backup of your namespace captures its objects (the VirtualMachine, its DataVolumes and PVCs, the Service) and its data: each disk is snapshotted, and the Data Mover copies the snapshot to object storage, so the backup survives even if the cluster's storage is lost. A running Windows VM is backed up crash-consistent unless the guest agent freezes it first: PostgreSQL recovers from that like from a power cut, and your hash chain proves it.

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm,dv,pvc,svc               # what your backup will contain
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get nonadminbackupstoragelocations.oadp.openshift.io 2>/dev/null || echo "(the class's location is the default one)"   # [verify]

💡 Use full resource names here. On these clusters oc get backup finds ODF's database-backup type and oc get restore finds ACM's, not OADP's. Several operators define a "backup" or "restore". Always write the full name, for example nonadminbackups.oadp.openshift.io or backups.velero.io.

docs.title: 5.2 Inject before the backup
docs.text:
alive                              # your VM is writing
mark d5-in-backup                  # ✍️ note the id: this row MUST come back
verify                             # chain_ok = t

In the VM's console (PowerShell):

Add-Content "C:\Users\Public\ovedr\$env:USERNAME.txt" "$(Get-Date -Format o)  d5-in-backup"

docs.title: 5.3 Back up your namespace
docs.text:
You create a NonAdminBackup in your own namespace; OADP turns it into a backup of that namespace only. [verify: the NonAdminBackup fields and the student rights on OADP 1.5 (demo-openshift reports what the operator grants)]

oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: oadp.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: NonAdminBackup
metadata: { name: d5 }
spec:
  backupSpec:
    snapshotMoveData: true        # the Data Mover: your disks' data leaves the cluster's storage
    ttl: 24h0m0s
EOF
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get nonadminbackups.oadp.openshift.io d5 -w            # Ctrl-C when its phase is Created and the backup Completed
mark d5-after-backup               # this row is NOT in the backup: it must be gone after the restore

Console: your project → Operators → Installed Operators → OADP → NonAdminBackup → Create.

✍️ Row 5.3: the backup's duration and size (oc -n "$VMNS" get nonadminbackups.oadp.openshift.io d5 -o yaml, under status).

docs.title: 5.4 Lose it: delete your VM
docs.text:
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" delete vm "$VM"                     # the VM and its disks are gone
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm,pvc                          # nothing left of your VM
alive                                                              # fails: that is the disaster

docs.title: 5.5 Restore, and prove the data
docs.text:
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: oadp.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: NonAdminRestore
metadata: { name: d5 }
spec:
  restoreSpec:
    backupName: d5                # your NonAdminBackup   [verify]
EOF
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get nonadminrestores.oadp.openshift.io d5 -w           # Ctrl-C when the restore Completed
oc --context site-a -n "$VMNS" get vm "$VM" -w                      # Running again
until alive >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 10; done; alive              # Windows booted, PostgreSQL recovered
verify                                                             # chain_ok = t
sql -c "SELECT stage FROM marks WHERE student = '$ME' AND stage LIKE 'd5-%' ORDER BY id;"

✅ d5-in-backup is back and chain_ok = t. d5-after-backup is gone: it was written after the backup, which is exactly what a restore means. Your file in the VM ends at d5-in-backup too.

✍️ Row 5.5: the restore's duration, chain_ok, and which of your rows came back.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: Before your class started, a CI pipeline built three environments and then customized them: operators, networks, storage, migration providers and maps, a namespace with a database client, one Windows + PostgreSQL VM per student, and a staged migration plan for each VM. This guide walks through every one of those pieces in the order CI builds them. For each piece you see what was built, how to check it, how to build it yourself from the command line, and how to do the same in the console, with links to the Red Hat documentation that describes it. The demo guides only ask you to do the last step yourself (start your migration). This guide is how you would do everything before it.

docs.title: How the lab is set up
docs.text:
Built by What Where demo-vmware (core-web dispatches it) vCenter vcenter0<N>, 4 nested ESXi hosts, the shared NFS datastore coresan01_data00, port group vm-network on VLAN 22+N, your vCenter folder vms/students/<your ID> vSphere lzN demo-openshift (core-web dispatches it, twice) OpenShift 4.19, OpenShift Virtualization (ove: cnv), ACM and cert-manager, NMState bridges + NADs per VLAN, nfs-csi storage; ODF on site A only site A <A> and site B <B> this demo's CI (customize, sections S.5–S.12) MTV, providers, maps, the class namespace, the class VMs, demo prep, the staged plans all three you start your own migration plan (Demo 1 / 1b), then everything in the demo guides

Picture: lab diagram. Every command below uses your class terminal's variables ($A, $B, $N, $VM, $DOMAIN; Toolkit T.1) and the contexts site-a / site-b. Most "do it yourself" steps need cluster-admin. In class you only read these objects; the instructor (or a cluster you own) can run the build steps.

export VLAN=$((22 + N))                 # the vSphere zone's VLAN: also the bridge your migrated VM can join

docs.title: S.1 The three environments, and what both clusters should look like
docs.text:
What CI built: core-web booked one vSphere zone and two OpenShift clusters together. Both clusters are built from the same member selections (ove: cnv, ACM, cert-manager), so they carry the same operators. The one difference is storage: the lab has four scratch SSDs, enough for one ODF cluster, so site A runs ODF and site B uses NFS (nfs-csi). The healthcheck compares the two sites' operators and reports any difference (ODF excluded).

Check:

for s in site-a site-b; do echo "== $s"; oc --context $s get csv -A --no-headers \
  | awk '{print $2}' | sed 's/\.v\{0,1\}[0-9].*$//' | sort -u; done
oc --context site-a get storageclass; oc --context site-b get storageclass

Console: Operators → Installed Operators, project All Projects, on each site. 📸 S-operators-site-a · 📸 S-operators-site-b: the two installed-operator lists side by side.

Red Hat docs: - OpenShift Container Platform 4.19 documentation - Operators: understanding OLM and installed operators - About OpenShift Virtualization

docs.title: S.2 OpenShift Virtualization (built by demo-openshift)
docs.text:
What was built: the OpenShift Virtualization operator (kubevirt-hyperconverged) in openshift-cnv, and its HyperConverged resource kubevirt-hyperconverged. That resource deploys KubeVirt, CDI (the disk importer), the templates and the boot sources.

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-cnv get hyperconverged kubevirt-hyperconverged \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Available")].status}{"\n"}'      # True
oc --context site-a -n openshift-cnv get csv | grep -i kubevirt

Do it yourself (CLI):

oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata: { name: openshift-cnv }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata: { name: kubevirt-hyperconverged-group, namespace: openshift-cnv }
spec: { targetNamespaces: [ openshift-cnv ] }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata: { name: hco-operatorhub, namespace: openshift-cnv }
spec: { source: redhat-operators, sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace, name: kubevirt-hyperconverged, channel: stable }
YAML
# once the CSV says Succeeded:
oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: hco.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: HyperConverged
metadata: { name: kubevirt-hyperconverged, namespace: openshift-cnv }
spec: {}
YAML

Console: 1. Operators → OperatorHub → search OpenShift Virtualization → Install (namespace openshift-cnv). 📸 S-cnv-operatorhub 2. Installed Operators → OpenShift Virtualization → Create HyperConverged → Create. 📸 S-cnv-hyperconverged 3. A Virtualization menu appears in the left navigation. 📸 S-cnv-menu

Red Hat docs: - Installing OpenShift Virtualization - Preparing your cluster for OpenShift Virtualization [verify link] - OpenShift Virtualization architecture [verify link]

docs.title: S.3 Networking: VLANs to bridges to network attachments
docs.text:
What was built (demo-openshift): the Kubernetes NMState operator, and on every node a Linux bridge br<VLAN> on the trunk NIC for each lab VLAN. Each bridge is a NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy (NNCP) named br<VLAN>-policy. In default there is a NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) vmnet<VLAN> that lets a VM plug into that bridge. The VLAN is the same one the vSphere port group vm-network uses, so a migrated VM can keep its address.

vSphere OpenShift port group vm-network, VLAN 22+N NNCP br<22+N>-policy → bridge br<22+N> → NAD default/vmnet<22+N>

Check:

oc --context site-a get nncp                                                   # br<VLAN>-policy … Available
oc --context site-a get nncp "br${VLAN}-policy" -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Available")].status}{"\n"}'
oc --context site-a -n default get net-attach-def "vmnet${VLAN}" -o jsonpath='{.spec.config}{"\n"}' | jq .

Do it yourself (CLI): install Kubernetes NMState Operator from OperatorHub, create its NMState instance, then:

TRUNK='<trunk NIC on the nodes, e.g. ens224>'          # [verify] the trunk interface name on your nodes
oc apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1
kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy
metadata: { name: br${VLAN}-policy }
spec:
  desiredState:
    interfaces:
      - name: ${TRUNK}.${VLAN}
        type: vlan
        state: up
        vlan: { base-iface: ${TRUNK}, id: ${VLAN} }
      - name: br${VLAN}
        type: linux-bridge
        state: up
        ipv4: { enabled: false }
        bridge: { options: { stp: { enabled: false } }, port: [ { name: ${TRUNK}.${VLAN} } ] }
---
apiVersion: k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1
kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
metadata: { name: vmnet${VLAN}, namespace: default }
spec:
  config: '{"cniVersion":"0.3.1","name":"vmnet${VLAN}","type":"bridge","bridge":"br${VLAN}","macspoofchk":true}'
YAML

Console: 1. Networking → NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy → Create (form or YAML), as above. 📸 S-nncp-create 2. Wait for Available on every node. 📸 S-nncp-available 3. Networking → NetworkAttachmentDefinitions → Create in default: type Linux bridge, bridge name br<VLAN>. 📸 S-nad-create

Red Hat docs: - Kubernetes NMState operator [verify link] - Connecting a VM to a Linux bridge network [verify link] - Multiple networks: NetworkAttachmentDefinition [verify link]

docs.title: S.4 Storage: whatever the booking chose, and snapshot classes
docs.text:
Storage is not this demo's choice. demo-openshift deploys each cluster's storage from its storage option (na = NFS, odf; other storage providers such as Portworx are forks of this class, BL-D25) and marks the class VMs belong on. CI's customize only reads that class (the storageclass.kubevirt.io/is-default-virt-class one, else the cluster default) and proves a test claim binds before any VM lands there. The demos work the same on any of them: they are about migration and BCDR.

# the class your VMs land on, per site (what CI's sc_live reads)
for s in site-a site-b; do
  oc --context $s get sc -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.metadata.annotations.storageclass\.kubevirt\.io/is-default-virt-class=="true")]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}'
done

What this booking's build has today: - Site A: OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF), Ceph on one scratch SSD per host. VMs use the storage class ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (block, RWX, so live migration works). Built by demo-openshift (storage: odf); core-web reserves the SSDs for the booking. - Site B: the same on the lab standard (storage: odf, ODF on the second SSD per host). A booking with odf-site-a gives site B only nfs-csi on the lab NFS server, and has no Demo 4. - Both sites also have nfs-csi (the cluster's default class; VMs default to the ODF virtualization class). - Snapshot classes come with the storage, from demo-openshift: nfs-csi-snapclass (driver nfs.csi.k8s.io) and ODF's own. Demo 1's snapshot bonus needs one. CI's demo-prep only reports a VM storage driver without one.

Check:

oc --context site-a get storageclass ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization
oc --context site-a -n openshift-storage get storagecluster      # Ready
oc --context site-b get storageclass nfs-csi
for s in site-a site-b; do oc --context $s get volumesnapshotclass; done

Do it yourself (CLI): a snapshot class for a driver that has none (what demo-openshift creates for NFS):

oc --context site-b apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata: { name: nfs-csi-snapclass }
driver: nfs.csi.k8s.io
deletionPolicy: Delete
YAML

ODF itself: install the OpenShift Data Foundation operator, label the storage nodes, and create a StorageSystem / StorageCluster on the local SSDs (the Local Storage operator discovers them).

Console: 1. Operators → OperatorHub → OpenShift Data Foundation → Install. 📸 S-odf-install 2. Storage → Data Foundation → Create StorageSystem → Create a new StorageClass using local storage devices. 📸 S-odf-storagesystem 3. Storage → StorageClasses: see ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (site A) and nfs-csi (site B). 📸 S-storageclasses 4. Storage → VolumeSnapshotClasses → Create. 📸 S-snapclass

Red Hat docs: - Deploying ODF using local storage devices [verify link] - Storage for virtual machines [verify link] - CSI volume snapshots [verify link]

docs.title: S.5 The Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV) operator
docs.text:
Who built it: the booking's migration_tools decides which sites get MTV (both: site A and site B; site-a: site B is left bare so students install MTV there). On those sites demo-openshift installs it (ove: cnv-mtv), and CI (ansible/roles/mtv_operator) checks it and customizes it for the class: - (demo-openshift) Namespace openshift-mtv, OperatorGroup migration (targets openshift-mtv), and Subscription mtv-operator: channel release-v2.11, source redhat-operators. CI waits for the CSV to report Succeeded. - (demo-openshift) ForkliftController/forklift-controller with feature_ui_plugin, feature_validation, feature_volume_populator and feature_must_gather_api all "true". (CI) adds controller_precopy_interval: "5" for Demo 2 and waits for deploy/forklift-controller to be Available. - (demo-openshift; CI re-checks) MTV's console plugin enabled in consoles.operator.openshift.io/cluster → spec.plugins. This is what adds the Migration for Virtualization menu. - Class access: RoleBinding ovedr-students-view (ClusterRole view) and Role + RoleBinding ovedr-students-migrate. The second lets students create, start and delete plans and migrations, and only read providers, maps and hosts. It never grants secrets.

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get subscription mtv-operator -o jsonpath='{.spec.channel}{"\n"}'   # release-v2.11
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get csv | grep mtv
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get forkliftcontroller,deploy/forklift-controller
oc --context site-a get console.operator cluster -o jsonpath='{.spec.plugins}{"\n"}'                    # includes forklift…
oc --context site-a auth can-i create plans.forklift.konveyor.io -n openshift-mtv                        # yes (students)

Do it yourself (CLI):

oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata: { name: openshift-mtv }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata: { name: migration, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { targetNamespaces: [ openshift-mtv ] }
---
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata: { name: mtv-operator, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { name: mtv-operator, channel: release-v2.11, source: redhat-operators, sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace }
YAML
oc -n openshift-mtv get csv -w                                  # wait for Succeeded, then:
oc apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: ForkliftController
metadata: { name: forklift-controller, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec:
  feature_ui_plugin: "true"
  feature_validation: "true"
  feature_volume_populator: "true"
  feature_must_gather_api: "true"
YAML
PLUGIN=$(oc get consoleplugin -o name | grep forklift | cut -d/ -f2); echo "$PLUGIN"
oc patch console.operator cluster --type json -p "[{\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/spec/plugins/-\",\"value\":\"$PLUGIN\"}]"

Console: 1. Operators → OperatorHub → Migration Toolkit for Virtualization Operator → Install, channel release-v2.11, namespace openshift-mtv. 📸 S-mtv-operatorhub 2. Installed Operators → MTV → ForkliftController → Create. 📸 S-mtv-forkliftcontroller 3. Accept "Web console update is available" and refresh. Migration for Virtualization appears in the menu. 📸 S-mtv-menu

Red Hat docs: - Installing and using the Migration Toolkit for Virtualization 2.11 [verify link] - MTV prerequisites [verify link] - Migration Toolkit for Virtualization 2.11 documentation

docs.title: S.6 The vSphere side: an MTV account, its role, and the vSphere provider
docs.text:
What CI built (automation/customize/mtv_fabric.sh): - On vCenter, an SSO user ovedr-mtv@vsphere.local, with a minted password stored in the class vault and never shown, and a role ovedr-mtv with MTV's minimal privilege set: - power on/off and guest control; - all of Provisioning; - create/remove snapshot; - ChangeTracking (CBT, for warm migration); - datastore browse and file management; - session validation; - Cryptographer decrypt/access.

It is granted on the vCenter root (/), propagating. CI checks the user can then list the inventory. - A network probe run from inside each cluster before any provider: vCenter 443, every ESXi host on 443 and 902 (MTV's disk copy), and the peer cluster's api-int 6443 and ingress 443. - On each tooled site, Secret + Provider/ovedr-vcenter0<N> (type vsphere, url https://vcenter0<N>…/sdk). It carries user, password, url and cacert: the certificate chain vCenter serves, so TLS is verified, never skipped. - VDDK: retired (2026-10-14). The lab has no VDDK image, so its migrations are cold (Demo 1). Warm migration (Demo 2) is coming soon with storage copy offload on a SAN array instead; why the lab dropped VDDK: Demo 2. S.15 is kept for reference.

Check:

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider "ovedr-vcenter0$N" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}  {.spec.url}{"\n"}'
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get provider "ovedr-vcenter0$N" -o jsonpath='{.spec.settings}{"\n"}'   # vddkInitImage?

Do it yourself (CLI): the vSphere role and user (govc, as a vCenter administrator), then the provider:

export GOVC_URL="https://vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN" GOVC_USERNAME='administrator@vsphere.local'   # GOVC_PASSWORD from your vault
govc role.create my-mtv VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOn \
  VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot VirtualMachine.State.RemoveSnapshot VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking \
  Datastore.Browse Datastore.FileManagement Sessions.ValidateSession   # … plus Provisioning.*, GuestControl, Cryptographer.*
govc sso.user.create -p '<password>' my-mtv        # the one place a password goes on argv: govc has no other way
govc permissions.set -principal my-mtv@vsphere.local -role my-mtv -propagate=true /

CA="$(openssl s_client -showcerts -servername "vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN" -connect "vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN:443" </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
      | sed -n '/-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----/,/-----END CERTIFICATE-----/p')"
oc -n openshift-mtv create secret generic my-vcenter --from-literal=user=my-mtv@vsphere.local \
  --from-literal=password='<password>' --from-literal=url="https://vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN/sdk" --from-literal=cacert="$CA" \
  --from-literal=insecureSkipVerify=false
oc -n openshift-mtv label secret my-vcenter createdForProviderType=vsphere createdForResourceType=providers
oc apply -f - <<YAML
apiVersion: forklift.konveyor.io/v1beta1
kind: Provider
metadata: { name: my-vcenter, namespace: openshift-mtv }
spec: { type: vsphere, url: "https://vcenter0$N.$DOMAIN/sdk", secret: { name: my-vcenter, namespace: openshift-mtv } }
YAML

Console: 1. vSphere Client: Administration → Roles → New (privileges as above); Single Sign On → Users and Groups → Add; Hosts and Clusters → vCenter → Permissions → Add. 📸 S-vsphere-role · 📸 S-vsphere-permission 2. OpenShift: Migration for Virtualization → Providers → Create Provider → VMware: URL, user, password, and either fetch certificate or paste the CA. 📸 S-mtv-provider-vsphere 3. The provider shows Ready, with VM and host counts. 📸 S-mtv-provider-ready

Red Hat docs: - VMware prerequisites and privileges for MTV [verify link] - Adding a VMware vSphere source provider [verify link] - Creating a VDDK image [verify link]

docs.title: S.7 OpenShift ⇄ OpenShift providers
docs.text:
What CI built: on both sites, ServiceAccount ovedr-mtv-peer in openshift-mtv (bound to cluster-admin, MTV's documented simplest grant for an OpenShift source; the cluster exists only for the booking) and a long-lived token Secret ovedr-mtv-peer-token. On each tooled site, a Provider ovedr-ocp-<peer> (type openshift) whose url and cacert both come from the peer's kubeconfig: the URL is https://api-int.<peer>…:6443 and the CA is the cluster's internal CA.

💡 Why api-int and not api? After demo-openshift's customize, api.<cluster> serves a public Let's Encrypt certificate. api-int keeps the cluster's internal CA. URL and CA must come from the same place, or TLS verification fails (x509: certificate signed by unknown authority). That happened in this lab, and it is why CI reads both from one kubeconfig.

Check:

oc --context site-b -n openshift-mtv get provider "ovedr-ocp-${A#ocp-}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}  {.spec.url}{"\n"}'

Do it yourself (CLI): on the source cluster, create the service account and token. On the destination, create the provider.

oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv create sa my-peer
oc --context site-a adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user cluster-admin -z my-peer -n openshift-mtv
oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
metadata: { name: my-peer-token, namespace: openshift-mtv, annotations: { kubernetes.io/service-account.name: my-peer } }
YAML
TOKEN="$(oc --context site-a -n openshift-mtv get secret my-peer-token -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d)"
URL="https://api-int.$A.$DOMAIN:6443"                  # match the CA below
